Abate

uh-BAYT -- ultimately from Latin ad- + battuere ('to beat'), the same root behind debate and combat. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To abate is to become less intense, severe, or widespread; to subside.

The protesters agreed to disperse once the mayor promised the new construction noise would abate before 9 p.m.

Worked Example

The doctor warned that the swelling might take two full days to abate, even with the medication.

The swelling doesn't disappear instantly -- it gradually becomes less severe over time, which is exactly what abate describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

subside: to become gradually less intense

wane: to decrease gradually in strength or extent

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

intensify: to become or make more severe or extreme

escalate: to increase rapidly in scale or intensity

Where it sits · how far the decline goes — subside → abate → wane

subside vs. abate: Subside is gentler than abate: applause subsides on its own within a minute, while we say a storm abates only when something truly severe finally loses its force.

wane vs. abate: Wane goes further than abate: a fever that abates has eased its grip for now, but enthusiasm that wanes keeps sinking steadily until little of it is left.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — a-

prefix — a-: to, toward (Latin (ad-))

root — -bate

root — -bate: to beat (Latin (battuere))

Put it together

Put it together: Abate comes from Old French abatre, built on Latin ad- ('to,' surfacing as a-) plus battuere ('to beat') -- something that abates has, in a sense, been 'beaten down' from its original force.

Use the root in a new word: debate

Use the root in a new word: debate: A debate is literally a 'beating down' of an argument -- from the same Latin root as abate, with de- ('down') added.

Root Check

Word Choice

Abate is most often used for things that build up and then gradually die down on their own -- storms, pain, fear, anger -- rather than things a person deliberately reduces.
